hints: Split the ester in your mind into its acid part and its alcohol part, then ask what single starting compound could supply both.
The target is propyl propanoate, so you need propanoic acid, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$, and propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. Check if propan-1-ol can give you both.
Now test propanal and propanone for the same trick: can each be oxidised to the acid and reduced to the primary alcohol in a school lab within four steps?
walkthrough:
**Split the ester into its two building blocks**

Think of ester formation as acid plus alcohol. Splitting the target helps you see what you must make.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Check statement 1: propan-1-ol as Z**

This is the simplest case. Keep some Z as the alcohol, oxidise the rest to the acid, then esterify. That is only two stages and uses Z as the only organic feedstock.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{[O]} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$$

**Check statement 2: propanal as Z**

Propanal sits in the middle of the oxidation ladder. Oxidise one batch up to propanoic acid, reduce another batch down to propan-1-ol, then esterify them together. That is three stages, still within the limit.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO} \xrightarrow{[O]} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO} \xrightarrow{[H]} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Check statement 3: propanone as Z**

Propanone is a ketone with the functional group on carbon 2. It resists oxidation in school conditions and reduces to propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, not the needed straight chain propan-1-ol or propanoic acid. So it cannot supply both parts.

Conclusion: 1 and 2 work, 3 does not.

options.A: This would mean 1, 2 and 3 are all possible. Statements 1 and 2 are possible, but 3 is not because propanone cannot be converted to propan-1-ol or propanoic acid by normal school oxidations and reductions.
options.B: This means 1 and 2 only are possible. Propan-1-ol can be partly oxidised to propanoic acid then esterified, and propanal can be oxidised one way and reduced the other way then esterified. Both routes need four reactions or fewer.
options.C: This would mean 2 and 3 only are possible. Statement 2 is correct but statement 3 is wrong and statement 1 is missing. Propanone fails while propan-1-ol clearly succeeds, so this combination is incorrect.
options.D: This would mean 1 only is possible. Statement 1 is indeed possible, but statement 2 is also possible and is wrongly excluded. Propanal is an excellent common precursor to both the acid and the alcohol.
